title: Turbulent channel: which grid gets the profiles right?
question: Case 17 got the mean speed of a turbulent channel flow right but missed its profiles. What is the cheapest grid on this PC that gets the profiles right too?
verdict_label: Every limit met, on one grid only

summary.headline: A grid with cells \(1.5\times\) finer along the flow and across it (\(288\times64\times96\)) meets all 10 limits of case 17. The first grid (\(192\times64\times64\)) met 5 of them: its mean speed was right, its profiles were not. The run on the new grid took \(1.7\) hours on the desktop GPU. It is one grid, with no finer one to confirm it.
summary.plain: A grid 1.5 times finer along and across the flow (288 x 64 x 96) meets all 10 limits of case 17 (the first grid met 5): mean speed +0.17 % with a statistical error of 0.19 %, in 1.7 GPU hours. One grid, no finer one to confirm it
reasons: the new grid is one grid, with no finer grid to confirm it: the last refinement along the flow still moved the mean speed by 0.8 per cent and the last across the flow by 0.6 per cent, in opposite directions
the time-step check of case 17 was not repeated on the new grid

Worst profile, as a share of its limit
answers.note: the first grid: \(173\,\%\) (above 100 % is a miss)

answers.label: GPU time of the run on the new grid

findings: The cells across the flow were the main problem. Making only them finer brought 4 of the 5 profiles inside their limits (Figure 3).
The cells along the flow come second. Making only them finer brought 2 profiles inside, and it moved the mean speed from \(-0.3\,\%\) to \(+0.8\,\%\).
Toward the wall the first grid was already fine enough: more cells there changed nothing.
The first grid's good mean speed was partly luck. Its two grid errors pushed in opposite directions and cancelled.
limitations: One grid, with no finer grid to confirm it. The last refinement in each direction still moved the mean speed by \(0.8\,\%\) and \(0.6\,\%\), in opposite directions, so the small difference from the reference again includes some cancellation.
The verdict of case 17 itself stays FAIL. That verdict belongs to the agent's solve; this study was made afterwards by the developer agent and stands next to it.
The three one-direction runs averaged only 10 time units each. They are good for ranking the directions, not for precise numbers.
One flow at one Reynolds number. The time-step check of case 17 was not repeated on the new grid.
summary.recommendation: For this flow on gpucfd, use cells of about 8 wall units along the flow and across it, and a first cell of one wall unit at the wall. Cells of 12 wall units are too coarse for the profiles.

setup.intro: The flow is water-like fluid pushed between two flat plates, fast enough to be turbulent: full of swirls that keep changing. The solver (gpucfd, the project's GPU program) computes every swirl directly. Two research groups published very exact results for this flow (Vreman and Kuerten 2014); that is the reference. All runs here are the same problem with the same settings. Only the grid differs.

terms.meaning: the box of fluid is cut into small cells, and the solver keeps one value per cell. It cannot see a swirl that is smaller than a cell. A grid is written as cells along the flow, toward the wall and across the flow.
how fast the fluid moves through the channel on average. One number.
a curve from the wall to the middle of the channel: how the velocity, or the strength of the swirls, changes with the distance from the wall. Harder to get right than the mean speed.
how strongly the velocity jumps around its average at one height (the root mean square of the fluctuation). There is one for each direction.
a speed built from the friction on the wall. All speeds on this page are multiples of it; the mean speed is about 15.7 of them.
the natural small length of the flow at the wall. Half the channel height is 180 wall units. The streaks of fast and slow fluid at the wall lie about 100 wall units apart.
the largest difference between our profile and the reference, anywhere along the profile.
how large a gap may be to pass. The solver agent of case 17 wrote the limits down before its runs; they were not changed here.
half the channel height divided by the friction velocity: roughly the time a large swirl needs to turn over once.
a turbulent flow never repeats, so an average over a finite time is a little uncertain. This number says by how much.

software: gpucfd, second order in space, implicit diffusion (imex)
chosen by the solver as the flow changes (Courant target \(0.75\))
Vreman and Kuerten 2014, mean of their two codes
fairness: Same problem, same solver settings and same pass limits in every run. Only the grid differs.
The limits and the reference are those of case 17, fixed before that case's runs.
The target, the budget and the rule for picking the new grid were written down before the first run of this study.
Not like for like: the first grid's result is an average over \(38\) time units, the new grid's over \(30\), the one-direction runs' over \(10\).

method.intro: First find out which direction of the grid is too coarse, with three short runs. Then make one full run on the cheapest grid that should pass, and judge it by the limits of case 17.

choices.choice: Refine one direction at a time
choices.why: Three short runs, each with the cells \(1.5\times\) finer in one direction only, show which direction matters. Refining everything at once would not say where the cells are needed.
choices.alternatives: Refine all three directions together: projected at about 4 GPU hours for one run, with nothing learned about where the cost can be saved.

choices.choice: Short runs of \(10\) time units for the three tests
choices.why: The gaps of the first grid are much larger than the scatter of a short average, measured beforehand on the first grid's own record (for the mean velocity \(0.019\) against a gap of \(0.31\)).
choices.alternatives: Long runs for each test: three times the cost for the same ranking.

choices.choice: Each run starts from the nearest finished flow field
choices.why: The field of the first grid is interpolated onto the new grid, so the flow is already turbulent. After 4 time units its speed is scaled once to where the wall friction says it is heading, and it settles for 3 more. This start-up takes 7 time units; the runs of case 17 needed about 20.
choices.alternatives: Start from rest with a disturbance, or wait for the mean speed to drift into place by itself.

choices.choice: Pick the new grid as the first grid plus the measured changes
choices.why: The cheapest grid whose predicted gaps all stay within 0.8 of their limits. For the picked grid the prediction is just the first grid's result plus the change measured for each of its two refinements.
choices.alternatives: A formula that assumes the error falls with the square of the cell size. It failed its own check here: these grids are too coarse for that rule (section 5).

choices.choice: The final run stops by a rule fixed beforehand
choices.why: It ends when the statistical error of the mean speed is below \(0.25\,\%\) after at least \(30\) time units, or after \(2\) GPU hours.
choices.alternatives: A fixed run length chosen by eye.

tables.result: Finer across the flow: 4 of 5 profiles inside. Finer along the flow: 2. Finer toward the wall: 0, with gaps as large as on the first grid.
tables.meaning: The cells across the flow matter most, because they must catch the thin streaks at the wall. The cells along the flow come second. Toward the wall nothing is gained, so the new grid keeps the first grid's cells there.
tables.note: Gaps in friction velocities; bold is outside its limit.

notes: With only the cells across the flow made finer, the swirl strength along the flow changes from too strong right at the wall to slightly too weak further out. It needs both refinements to come inside its limit.
The mean speed barely shows any of this. It is the profiles that tell a resolved flow from an unresolved one.

sections.title: How sure is this result?
sections.intro: Meeting the limits on one grid is not the same as knowing the answer has stopped changing. Three checks say how far this result can be trusted.

tables.result: No. Each last step still moved the mean speed by more than half a per cent, in opposite directions.
tables.meaning: About half a per cent of grid error is probably left from each direction, and the two partly cancel. The mean speed of the new grid is trustworthy to about half a per cent, not to the \(0.17\,\%\) it happens to show. A finer grid would settle it.
tables.note: The estimate assumes the error falls with the square of the cell size, which these grids do not fully obey. The run with finer cells along the flow only had not fully settled, so the second row is less certain.

tables.result: Four of the five profiles came out close to the prediction. The mean velocity came out better than predicted.
tables.meaning: Adding up the changes measured one direction at a time is a usable guide for picking a grid, and no more than that.

notes: The original plan was a formula that splits each gap into shares of the three directions. Its own check failed: carried to infinitely fine cells it does not go to zero. So it was used only to rank the directions.

tables.result: The new grid has \(2.25\times\) the cells of the first grid and costs \(2.6\times\) as much per time unit.
tables.meaning: A resolved run of this flow fits in under two hours on this PC. The whole study took \(3.1\) GPU hours of the \(5\) set aside.

notes: Making the cells finer across the flow lowers the number of steps per time unit: the better resolved flow has milder extremes, so the solver may take longer steps.
The cheap option: finer across the flow only costs \(1.3\times\) the first grid and brings 4 of the 5 profiles inside.
